segments.t: Realizing that the neighboring Italian restaurant, Arcobaleno, ordered the fake fire inspection, Dmitry decides to take revenge. He angrily calls the immigration service with a fake complaint against his rivals. Let us listen to their conversation in Russian first.
Now let us examine the conversation line by line.
'Do you want a war?' Nagiyev turns a statement into a question purely through rising intonation on the word meaning 'want', followed by 'the war'.
'There will be a war for you.' Nagiyev chooses the imperfective verb meaning 'will be' for the ongoing action, followed by 'a war'.
'Hello, good afternoon.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'hello?' directly with 'good', combining 'hello?' with 'good' and 'day'.
'For what do they pay you money?' Dmitry uses the polite plural 'you' alongside 'money', keeping a formal or respectful register.
'Where are you looking?' The question word for 'where to' comes right at the start, followed directly by 'look'.
'There are migrants in my courtyard.' Russian omits the present-tense verb 'to be' here, linking 'yard' directly with 'migrant', combining 'yard' with 'migrant'.
'From the restaurant Arcobaleno.' Nagiyev delivers a punchy one-word reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'restaurant'.
'They are slaughtering a live ram.' Nagiyev chooses the imperfective verb meaning 'cut' for the ongoing action, followed by 'a living' and 'ram'.
'And are you sleeping there?' Nagiyev leads with the direct command form meaning 'to sleep', followed by 'there'.
'Come quickly.' Nagiyev chooses the imperfective verb meaning 'to come' for the ongoing action, followed by 'quickly'.
'Arcobaleno.' Nagiyev delivers a punchy one-word reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'Arcobaleno'.
'What are you doing?' Chef Barinov delivers a punchy one-word reaction built around the Russian word meaning 'are you doing'.
'I am solving our problems.' Nagiyev chooses the imperfective verb meaning 'decide' for the ongoing action, followed by 'problems'.

'Well done, keep it up.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the line on the word meaning 'well done' and builds the thought around 'to keep'. Now let's listen to the whole conversation again from start to finish.

Furious at his rivals at Arcobaleno, Chef Barinov declares war and calls the migration service with a dramatic complaint to retaliate against the neighboring restaurant. Next time you watch the episode, listen for the Russian expressions for 'to want' and 'war' — you will catch every word right away. See you in the next scene.
